one_liner: Tracing JIT for the Wren scripting language on SLJIT; beats LuaJIT on a few microkernels but loses on 9 of 10 Benchmarks Game ports.
what_it_does: WrenJIT patches the stock Wren VM (pinned at 99d2f0b) with JIT hooks (patches/0001-wren-jit-hooks.patch) and adds a trace compiler that turns hot Wren loops into native code through SLJIT. Embedders keep the normal wren.h API (wrenNewVM, wrenInterpret); the JIT is switched with wrenJitSetEnabled from the internal header, or compiled out with -DWREN_JIT=OFF. It runs Wren programs only; it is not a Lua or general-purpose JIT.
how_it_is_fast: Loops: after 50 backward LOOP hits at one PC (JIT_HOT_THRESHOLD) one iteration is recorded as typed SSA, run through about 20 passes (box/unbox elimination, GVN, LICM, guard hoisting, integer induction-variable inference, bounds-check hoisting, escape analysis, comparison/guard fusion), linear-scan allocated and emitted via SLJIT, with snapshot-based side exits back to the interpreter. Several passes are closed-form or pattern rewrites: pass 15 replaces a boolean-toggle counter loop with arithmetic, pass 16 replaces an integer range sum with (limit-iter)*(iter+limit+1)/2, and pass 18 (irOptDenomRecurrence) turns the spectral-norm A(i,j) denominator into a running recurrence. Recursion: called functions are matched against exact bytecode shapes (byte count and opcode positions) and replaced by native kernels for binary Fibonacci, Takeuchi (real int64 native recursion), linear recursion (collapsed to a loop), mutual parity (one AND), Ackermann (closed forms for small m) and binary-tree make/check (hand-written C in wren_jit_recursion.c).
when_to_use: You already embed Wren and have hot numeric loops over ranges, lists or object fields that you want to run several times faster than the Wren interpreter (author's report: spectral-norm 652.8 to 17.0 ms, mandelbrot 701.9 to 68.3 ms, pidigits 1190.2 to 66.4 ms on Apple M4 Pro).
Research or teaching: a compact (about 10,000 lines across the seven JIT source files read) tracing JIT with SSA IR, guard snapshots and per-pass debug dumps (WREN_JIT_DUMP_IR, WREN_JIT_DEBUG).
ARM64 or x86-64 hosts, which are the only tested targets.
when_not_to_use: You want to beat LuaJIT on real programs: on the author's own ten Benchmarks Game ports WrenJIT is slower on 9 of 10 (nbody 848.4 vs 31.8 ms, regex-redux 455.9 vs 23.9 ms, k-nucleotide 175.4 vs 30.9 ms); only pidigits wins (66.4 vs 119.8 ms).

Production use: one author, 29 commits, 4 stars, no releases; no side traces or trace chaining (one trace per loop PC), so branchy loops keep exiting to the interpreter (fannkuch-redux logged 30,219,029 side exits in bench/benchmarksgame_results.json).
General recursive code: there is no method JIT, only six recognised bytecode shapes; anything else runs in the stock interpreter.
Code that must stay correct for any input program: the shape matchers for the recursive kernels do not check operator or call-target symbols (see gotchas).
Platforms other than ARM64 and x86-64, or builds without CMake and Git submodules.

integration.form: static lib (wrenjit_vm, the patched Wren VM plus JIT) built with CMake; CLI runner wrenjit_cli
integration.dependencies: Wren (git submodule pinned at 99d2f0b, patched by scripts/setup.sh) and SLJIT (submodule pinned at d9902b1); pthread and libm
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler (GCC, Clang or AppleClang flags in CMakeLists.txt), CMake 3.16+; Release builds use -O3 and IPO/LTO when supported
integration.platforms: ARM64 and x86-64 tested (README Limits); report measured on Apple M4 Pro
integration.thread_safety: not documented (JIT state lives in the per-VM vm->jit; Wren VMs are single-threaded)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces the stock Wren VM behind the same wren.h embedding API, but it runs only Wren, so it is not a drop-in for LuaJIT or Lua code

gotchas: Correctness bug by code reading (not run here): the recursive matchers for binary Fibonacci, linear recursion, Ackermann and Takeuchi in src/jit/wren_jit_recursion.c check opcode positions, integer constants and that both call sites use the same module variable and symbol, but never check which operator symbols are called (<, -, +, ==, !) or that the call target is the function itself; only the tree and mutual-parity kernels resolve names. A hot static method with the same bytecode shape but different operators or callee (for example `return Other.g(n - 1) * Other.g(n - 2)`, or `if (n > 2)`) would be replaced by the Fibonacci kernel after 50 calls with integer arguments, despite the README's 'validates constants, symbols, arity'.

Five of the nine README microbenchmark rows (range for, method call, ack, mutual recursion, deep recursion) run closed-form or loop-collapsed replacements and binary trees runs hand-written C (treeMakeFill bypasses the constructor), while LuaJIT runs the real loops and calls; fib and tak are real recursion but in specialised int64 native kernels with no type checks inside, so even those rows compare a hand-shaped kernel with LuaJIT's general JIT.

bench/run_benchmarks.py only parses each program's self-reported 'elapsed:' line; it never compares Wren and Lua outputs, or JIT and no-JIT outputs, so a miscompile would not show up in the benchmark run (the upstream Wren test suite and test/test_jit.c run under ctest instead).

By code reading, pass 16 (irOptFastForwardRangeSum) keeps the body nodes before the sum add for one execution and deletes every node after it up to the back edge, with no check that the body holds nothing else; whether other passes stop such traces is not documented. Also the JIT can be slower than the interpreter: the earlier Benchmarks Game run shows fannkuch-redux 11,430 vs 7,124 ms, fasta 182 vs 75 ms and regex-redux 765 vs 518 ms with JIT on.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only when you are committed to Wren and want its hot loops faster; for Lua code LuaJIT itself wins on 9 of the 10 paired ports, and Apogee (Lua 5.5 with a JIT in pure Go) is the sibling that measures honestly against a reference interpreter across 17 benchmarks rather than against LuaJIT on shaped kernels. Among new-language JITs, stryke and Objeck also claim LuaJIT wins on a minority of rows, so none of these is a general LuaJIT replacement.
verified_claims_summary: On an Apple M4 Pro (2026-08-07, best of five, both sides self-timed with clock()-based CPU time, process startup excluded, Wren timer includes JIT compilation, C compiler not named, LuaJIT build flags not stated) WrenJIT beat LuaJIT 2.1 on nine paired microkernels from 0.76x (fib 35: 39.4 vs 51.9 ms) to 0.02x (ack 3,7), but most rows time closed-form or hand-written replacements; on the author's ten Benchmarks Game ports (2026-08-08, LuaJIT 2.1.1785763465) it won only pidigits (66.4 vs 119.8 ms) and lost the rest by 1.58x to 26.69x.
status_note: Active single-author research project (last commit 2026-08-14, 29 commits, MIT); usable as a Wren VM replacement for experiments, but the shape-matched recursive kernels need symbol and callee checks before it is trusted on arbitrary programs.
